Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, it is obvious of
course from the language of the motion that it was placed upon the order paper prior to the first day of March. It will be necessary, when the house is in committee, to give effect to the principle of extending the time for the operation of the statute to May 1, by amending the words that are used.
Last year it will be recalled that this parliament enacted a statute whereby certain powers were conferred upon the governor in council to deal with unemployment and farm relief. It is well to keep in mind the provisions of the preamble of that measure, for they indicate clearly the constitutional division between the rights of parliament and the rights of provincial legislatures. The duties and obligations that fall upon provincial legislatures, under our constitution, are largely though not wholly defined by section 92 of the British North America Act. The balance, or remainder or residue of powers, including those specifically named in section 91, rest in this parliament, and it will be observed that words used in the preamble of the statute passed last year are:
.... and whereas it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and other bodies in such ways as the governor in council may deem expedient, and for that purpose should vest in the governor in council the powers necessary to insure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of all relief measures and the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada ....
That is a very concise and clear statement of the constitutional position of this parliament. It was so stated, of course, in 1930, and was agreed upon, I think, by all parties in the house in statements made from time to time during the course of the debate. The

Unemployment Continuance Act
primary obligations rest with the municipalities and the .provinces; the duty of parliament, in a national crisis or in a great emergency, is to assist and supplement the efforts of the provincial authorities.
I mention that because there seems to have been, judging from some of the questions asked within the past few days, a very distinct misunderstanding with respect to this phase of the question. I observed, for instance, that questions were asked as to why the Dominion government did not deal with the problem of seed and fodder. Obviously that obligation does not rest upon the Dominion government; it rests, of course, on the provincial authorities, acting either directly or through the city, town or municipal authorities which have been set up.
In this regard I think it perhaps desirable, although I did not so intend until yesterday, to read to the house a statement of the law as defined by the late Lord Chancellor Haldane in two cases that went to the privy council from this dominion. One was the case in which this parliament set up the court of commerce, which was to regulate prices of commodities and deal with the rights of traders; the other was the case in which, after the war, the Dominion government conferred upon an official power to fix the price of newsprint, and it was contended by the Winnipeg Free Press that no such power rested with the parliament of Canada but that the power to regulate prices, arising out of property and civil rights, must of necessity, be a matter solely within the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities. I think it well, therefore, in order that there may be a clear statement of the position placed upon Hansard, to read a few words from the judgment of Viscount Haldane in the court of commerce case, supplemented by a brief reference to his judgment in the Free Press paper control ease.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Then let us say it is
correct in the way in which the hon. gentleman said it at the meeting in question. Now, it has been contended that the suggestions thus sought were not acted upon. Well, it was idle to expect that all the suggestions offered could be acted upon. But I believe it will be found that, regardless of political considerations in any way, shape or form, employment was given to those who needed employment to the fullest possible extent, having regard to the fact that the government determined that it would not embark upon a wholesale expenditure of public moneys merely because suggestions were made that would involve that being done. That is fundamentally clear. If all the suggestions which were made were placed before this house they would give to the country a composite picture of a desire to enter upon unbridled extravagance to an extent wholly out of keeping with our present economic condition.
Then we went to the next phase. We approached the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and the western provinces and dealt with them in the same manner. There then came up the question of determining how we could best supplement and assist the provinces in the discharge of their constitutional obligations. We sought to assist the provinces regardless entirely of the political affiliations of those who directed the administrations. Much comment has been made in this house in connection with conditions in British Columbia. That government was Conservative and the contention has been made that we did not fall in with all the suggestions made by the province. That is not untrue; it is correct because we were unable to do so. At least some commendation has come from quarters usually lacking in praise of the action taken in that regard. The province of Quebec, a Liberal government, formulated an extensive program which it sought to have carried out by the joint operation of the provincial and federal authorities and in some instances with the aid of the municipalities. These representations were canvassed and in the end an agreement was arrived at, which agreement will be laid upon the table of this house. The same applies to the province of Ontario, to the western provinces and to the Pacific province of British Columbia.
That is a method by which we endeavoured to give effect to our constitutional duties, to supplement, under the conditions which existed, the legislative power which this parliament had conferred upon it. Complaints were received from time to time. In some instances it was contended that only Liberals were being employed; in other instances it

was contended that only the supporters of former governments were being employed, and in others, that only Conservatives were being employed. In the end, to meet this situation as best we could-it being a difficult situation at best-we asked reasonably responsible men to observe and report upon the work being done, to see that the effort was commensurate with the money being expended and to see that the work stipulated for was being performed according to the terms of the contract.
I submit to this house that in the main we have had remarkable success in dealing with this problem. I will go a step further. We have expended moneys which were appropriated directly for that purpose under the control financially of the Auditor General and of all the departmental engineers responsible for such expenditure-Public Works here, Railways there and Department of Interior works here. These departments and their officials along with the Auditor General's check upon expenditures have been responsible for the work being carried on. As to the work done by the provinces, we had no power to say that it should be done at the least possible initial expense so far as the appropriation was concerned. We told them that we would not pay any part of the administration cost; we told them that the cities and towns would have to pay that. We told them that as they had shovels, picks and other facilities which could be utilized for giving effect to their undertakings, they should be used. We told the Department of National Defence that it should lend its tents and other facilities of that kind to enable the work to be carried on in the national parks. That was done. With the minimum of new material and the maximum utilization of facilities which we had, the work was carried out expeditiously. I shall not read from the report which I have because it would not be fair to those who may follow me and who have not this document before them. I had hoped that this document would have been available to all before I made this statement.
While there always has been and always will be difficulties in connection with public expenditures by reason of the fact that there are men and women who will always think it desirable to get something for no effort from government, and that to impose upon government is a virtue and not a vice, I contend that in the main millions of dollars of public money have been expended fairly since this parliament adjourned in August last until to-day. As nearly one hundred cents for the

Unemployment Continuance Act
dollar as it is possible to get in public expenditure has been obtained, and much employment has been given to those who needed it. If at times there have been causes for complaint, as there have been, we have endeavoured to rectify whatever difficulties or whatever wrongs existed as expeditiously as possible. At the end of this period we face this parliament with some sense of pride in the fact that these vast undertakings have given employment to over 300,000 men working over 6,000,000 hours. While that does not mean that each man has had long work, while it does not mean that each had many hours of work, it means that by the judicious rotation of the work and by the giving of employment for a half day or a longer period, we have been able to accord that which we started out to accord, namely, relief to a large number of those who demanded and required it. That is what we endeavoured to do and that is what we did do. Our duty and our obligation were to provide relief, and that is what we endeavoured to do through the medium of the provinces.
We did not come in direct contact with the municipalities; our contact was through the provinces because the municipalities are the creation of the provinces. A still greater difficulty became apparent in September, that is, that the municipalities and the provinces could not undertake to provide the necessary finances to enable them to defray the expenses they had incurred. Not being able so to do, what was to happen? There was only one thing, that we should lend them the money which they could not otherwise borrow. This government in the exercise of the powers conferred upon it under the statute made loans to the provinces for the purpose of enabling them to discharge their obligations under their agreements and for the purpose of enabling the municipalities to discharge their contractual obligations. This money was loaned at the rate of interest which it had cost us. In response to a question asked a few days ago there has been laid upon the table of this house a statement indicating the sums of money which have been loaned. For instance, at the end of February the province of Saskatchewan had been advanced over $16,800,000; the loans to Alberta amounted to more than $4,600,000; the loans to Ontario were in the form of advances which have been offset by accounts for which we are liable with the exception of $190,000; the loans to British Columbia amounted to $5,600,000 and to Manitoba, $3,775,000.
Those represent moneys that were advanced by the dominion for the purpose of enabling the provinces to meet their constitutional
obligations, except with respect to the province of Saskatchewan about which I shall presently speak and the province of Ontario where an advance was made which was paid by credits which they were entitled to receive under their agreement, and which credits have entirely wiped out the advance that was made.
The obligation which was not one we ourselves assumed but which was one we had to assume if the work was to be carried on, wa3 an obligation that came upon us by reason of the economic conditions that prevailed in consequence of the disruption of the financial structures of the world after Great Britain went off the gold standard. Now I ask the chamber and particularly hon. members opposite if they have any complaint to make with regard to the manner in which we have met those responsibilities. We found every one of the four western provinces, for reasons which I shall not discuss, unable to secure money with which to discharge their obligations in New York. Were we to let those provinces default, or were we to lend them the necessary money with which to meet their obligations? Is there any hon. member who will stand up in his place and say: You should have let them default. That is the problem which confronted us-default or a loan. Is there any hon. member present who would suggest that we should have chosen the former alternative and not the latter? While some hon. members may suggest that it is undesirable to make advances to the provinces under the conditions that prevail, there is no member sitting either to the left or to the right of the Speaker who does not realize the fact that if any province, however small, wherever located, defaulted, this would injuriously affect the credit of Canada as a whole, and what is more, adversely affect beyond any words that I might use, the future of the people of this country.

Were the sums that were
advanced to the provinces taken from the proceeds of the service loan?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
That includes the amounts mentioned by my hon. friend as lent to the provinces?

speechtext:
Yes, prior to the end
of February. I fancy an illustration will serve the purpose of my hon. friend who has just asked me the question, as we both come from Alberta. In January, for instance, we provided $320,000 to meet the interest on the maturing New Y'ork obligation of Alberta and on the thirteenth of the same month we provided $2,822,000 for a loan also due in that city.

The province of Manitoba had an obligation amounting to 82,000,000 maturing in New York and we renewed ithe obligation for $1,000,000 and paid 81,000,000 on account. We also incurred at that very time the responsibility for paying that renewal at the date of maturity.
I now come to the second branch of our activities which arose out of the situation existing in Saskatchewan. It will be within the memory of most members of the house that on Dominion day of last year I referred to the condition which prevailed in that province. Saskatchewan is largely an agricultural province; it has a population of slightly over 900,000 souls. Seventy-six municipalities with a population numbering several hundred thousand have, for three successive seasons, been without a crop, and the soil, alluvial in character, fertile beyond words, has become so disintegrated by reason of the fibres being broken, that it is blown about by every wind that passes over the area in question. The soil that once was bright with verdure is now dark and as barren of vegetation as the floor. This, may I say to the chamber, has brought about the largest problem that the Canadian people have ever had to face. I wonder how many people at the maximum does this house think were actually fed during this winter in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is
quite right-something over 300,000. I put it to my fellow Canadians if they know of any major task Canadians ever discharged with greater efficiency and less noise? It was effectually, efficiently done, and what is more, with medical services, with plain but ample food, with fuel, over 300,000 people at the maximum, or nearly one-third of the population of Saskatchewan, were taken care of in that province this winter.

By the provincial or the
federal government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am coming to that. In that instance we did just what I said a moment ago: we asked the provincial authorities to set up a commission, which they did, presided over by a gentleman of means who is giving his services voluntarily, assisted, I am proud to say, by a member of the profession to which I belong, who, day after day and week after week, abandoning his own business, has been giving of his great abilities to the solution of the problems that have arisen. We also had representatives there for the purpose of assisting them. If Canadians have cause to be proud of anything, it is of 
the fact that through various organizations, such as the Red Cross and other associations of that character, by the free and voluntary gifts of men and women in eastern Canada to their less fortunate fellow citizens in the west, there have been sent not less than ninety-nine carloads of vegetables, clothing, other commodities of various kinds for free distribution amongst the people in that area and other parts of Saskatchewan. The churches offered to undertake part of that work; they did it and they did it well. The other day I heard of a case where a man of some means obtained some jars of jam which were being distributed, to which it was thought he had no claim, and indeed he had none. I do not dispute the soundness of the criticism; I mention it merely as indicating that is only a small matter when one considers the large, broad question of a commisison functioning with the aid and assistance of your government, whereby upwards of 300,000 men, women and children in peace time, were provided with the necessities of life, cared for during the winter and now, at the beginning of March find themselves at least in health and strength and, I am bound to say, with an optimism and courage with respect to the future that would shame some of us who live under different conditions. I shall not go further into the details of this effort, but I have no doubt that it is one in which hon. gentlemen opposite will feel, as we all do, a sense of pride, that a condition so strange in the life of a country, that privation and suffering that might have been so dreadful, have been met as they have.

Did the money go directly
from the federal treasury to the relief commission or to the province?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
By arrangement made
with the province and with the banks we deposited the money in the banks to the credit of the relief commission, the credits being made in this fashion:

All of which we have paid. Believing that we were but giving voice and effect to the wishes of this parliament the government

Unemployment Continuance Act
undertook the payment of 100 per cent of the relief thus afforded in those communities where there had been no crop for three successive years, because the municipalities and provinces were in such financial conditions that, I need hardly mention to this house, they could make no contribution at all. .
In that regard reference has been made to the fact that promissory notes were signed by which they undertook to repay the sums so advanced. Well, sir, I will tell this house exactly what was done, because that is one of the instances in connection with which I remained long enough in Regina to take some personal interest in the procedure, and to lay down what I conceived to be the proper rules which should govern in determining how relief should be granted. First, a survey was made of every municipality; it was not guess work, but made by men employed for that purpose who visited every settler, taking from each one a statement of what he had, of his financial position, and asking him to sign a declaration as to the truthfulness of the statements thus made. That was No. 1.
No. 2: An estimate was made by the settler himself as to what he would require, not as money, but for the purpose of meeting the demands made upon him and his family for food, fuel, clothing and matters of that kind and, sir, it was my privilege at the beginning of the year to visit one of the depots from which clothing was being distributed. When I saw the character of the requests being made, and the care with which apparently those who asked for assistance indicated their requirements, I realized that here was a people who were not taking an opportunity to provide themselves with things they did not require, but were asking those things necessary to meet only their most urgent requirements, having regard to the conditions under which they were living.
Then the question arose as to whether or not they should sign promises to repay what had been expended. That is debatable; there are those who hold the view that they should not be required to do so. I have no complaint to make, whatever view is held. However, the settlers affected were most insistent, the ones with whom we came most in contact, that they should be permitted to sign an undertaking to repay.

Do many of them not
deny that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have no doubt some
deny it', but I am speaking only from what I myself was told by settlers I met in Regina. Whether or not that feeling was general, I
am not in a position to say; naturally I have to take the reports which come to me. I must say, however, I never witnessed a finer spirit on the part of men and women who had homes, mark you-good homes-who had homes which had been in their possession for ten years, fifteen years or twenty years, who had barns, sheds, fences, wells and equipment but who for three years had had no crops, whose resources were gone. They had, however, a natural pride which belongs to the race and breed from which they sprang to desire not to accept charity but to accept a loan from the people which one day they might repay. For my part I have no objection to offer to criticism and I suspect from what I heard in Regina that the relation between the loan and the promise to pay is not greatly different from that of cause and effect. I still think it was not an improper thing to do, because let me say that since August, 1930, it has been my unfortunate experience sitting at the treasury board to have placed before me at almost every meeting, anywhere from ten to one hundred cases in regard to which the commission, as the hon. ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) will remember, was set up to deal with seed grain, feed and relief expenditures made in the northwest territories and the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta during periods of time which are now long past. Some of them go back to the years 1901, 1902, 1903, 1904 and 1905, and all along the years, because as I told the house last year there have been very few years since 1870, when relief on some scale has not been granted in western Canada, when that part of Canada was still territories. For, as territories, it will be recalled they were, in a sense, wards of this dominion, and we took the responsibility which under the constitution now rests with the provinces.
We are now confronted with the next problem, that of providing the seed for the cropping or sowing of those vast areas. Of course ever since last fall we have been endeavouring to ascertain just what the future would likely be. We have received from those most vitally affected a statement as to what they believed-having regard to their knowledge of conditions and the history of the past as to moisture and the general turn of events whereby we have cycles of crops, and so on- the future might reasonably be, so far as crops in a particular area were concerned. We have asked the premiers of the three prairie provinces for their views. We have asked them what assistance they will require to enable them to provide seed and feed, and
906	COMMONS
Unemployment Continuance Act
the supplies with which to put in a crop. Then as to fuel-whether it be used for mechanical appliances, traction engines, or oats and hay for horses-whatever it may be-we have asked them to give us estimates of the cost. The province of Alberta has taken great care to endeavour to spread out their resources to the limit of their power, and their estimate is that if they are provided with $140,000 it will be sufficient for the areas which under normal conditions they would take care of but which at the present time they cannot do without some assistance. In the province of Manitoba we were advised that something less than $700,000 would take care of requirements. When we come to the province of Saskatchewan however we must consider that there are upwards of 4,000,000 acres of land upon which we have to determine as best we can, with the aid and assistance of the best experts available, what to do.
As no doubt hon. members are aware, in the United States there has been placed a limitation upon the acreage which will be seeded. That limitation is based upon what has been done in previous years. A sum was recently voted by congress for the purpose of extending credits, and hon. members will recall that something like $50,000,000 is to be made ivailable for purposes I am now discussing. A. limitation however has been placed upon the amount which may be advanced in any specific case either for food, seed, fuel or fodder.
The federal authorities feel that they are not in as good a position as the provinical authorities to arrive at a proper judgment. Therefore we have concluded that instead of doing what has been done in days gone by, merely undertaking the responsibility for seed and feed as a national or dominion obligation, we will advance the necessary moneys by way of loans to the three provinces on their treasury bills, to enable them to provide seed and feed to fulfil the requirements of their agrarian populations. It may interest this house to know that we took steps last year to acquire through the aid of Mr. McFarland- who has so generously and freely without salary or compensation given of his time in the management of the wheat pools-sufficient quantities of wheat to take care of that situation at a price which I should say is at least ten cents lower than the rate to-day prevailing. That will be of some assistance to those who have to place their crops in the soil. It will require approximately for all purposes, for seed and feed, whether you use it to purchase hay or oats, or fuel oil or gasoline to put in the crop, approximately six million 
dollars to care for the requirements of Saskatchewan.
This, then, is the situation that confronts us. I have endeavoured to indicate to the house as clearly as I could in broad and general terms, without trespassing too much upon its time, the sweep of our undertakings and the general principles that have governed us in the administration of the statute that was passed last session. But this government have had a greater sense of their responsibilities because of the fact that we were vested with larger powers. In practice, I may say, we realize now that the statute that conferred these powers upon the government without naming the amount available was vastly to the advantage of this dominion, and had it been otherwise we could not have accomplished the purposes that we did accomplish without the expenditure of much more money. That is our profound conviction, and it is the opinion of the business men with whom we come in contact.

Are the sums which my right hon. friend has said have been placed to the credit of the relief commission in Saskatchewan for the purpose of relief a part of the moneys advanced to the province, or are they contributions from the federal government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I thought, Mr. Speaker,
I had made myself clear when I said that the grand total of the sum advanced to Saskatchewan was $16,800,000, but of that sum $5,250,000 represented advances-all expended at this time-to the relief commission, which will not be repaid to us, and which, as I said last session speaking in this house, was a contribution made by Canada to a national emergency on a scale-may I say?-which we Canadians have never heard of before.
Does that mean when those notes are repaid the money will not come back to this government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I say so far as we
are concerned, we have not received any treasury bills from the province of Saskatchewan for the repayment of these amounts, neither have we sought them.
Five million dollars?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Exactly. That is a
matter for future consideration and adjustment. It was discussed at some length the other day by hon. gentlemen.
Is that amount represented by the notes taken from the farmers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Whether or not notes
have been given for the full five million

What relief has been

dollars I cannot say. My own opinion would be that there are not notes for any such sum as that. But as far as we are concerned, we have advanced that money to the province for the purpose I have indicated, and, as I have said, to the extent to meet the whole one hundred per cent of cost because the province is not in a condition at the moment to make any contribution to it.

To whom are those
notes payable?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I understand it, to
the commission. I was indebted the other day to the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) for seeing one of those notes for the fust time. I think it read:	To His Majesty's
government in right of the dominion.
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a matter, however, that will have to be dealt with and adjusted in the future. I merely mention it in passing because at the moment the expenditure for seed and feed advances is to be covered by the treasury notes of all the three provinces in order that we may be able to meet the situation that exists.
In this case it is expected that all the advances for seed and relief to carry the people through the summer will be repaid by the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
So far as the immediate
advances are concerned, we are at the moment taking the treasury notes of the provinces and treating them all on the same basis; but, as I ventured to say the other day, and I now repeat, all this must necessarily be a matter for adjustment, but left in such shape that there can be at least no cause for complaint on the part of any person however careful he may be in regard to the expenditure of the nation's money. That is the position up to that point.

I think the right hon. gentleman stated that altogether the federal government had advanced something like $16,000,000 to the province of Saskatchewan, and that out of the $16,000,000 some $5,250,000 was advanced to the relief commission. Am I right in saying that the province of Saskatchewan, treating it as a corporate body, would owe the federal government $11,000,000, because the other $5,250,000 was advanced to the relief commission as a separate amount and the province therefore is not responsible with respect to it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are some limitations. but in a broad and general way that is a correct statement of it in figures.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The relief which in the
judgment of the provinces and municipalities was necessary to meet the situation. In the province of Saskatchewan a relief commission was set up, but broadly no relief commissions have been set up in any other province, although there has been a cooperative effort on the part of voluntary organizations with the municipalities and the provinces. The amount and extent of the relief are not matters over which the dominion exercises control, except, I trust, by way of kindly suggestion; the provinces determine what they should do.
Is the $6,000,000 included in the $11,000,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

That is a straight loan to
Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is a straight loan
for the present, but, as I said to the hon. member for Weyburn, all these matters must in the very necessity of things be matters for discussion and adjustment when the crisis ia passed. When we were confronted with the situation the question we had to consider was how we would meet it, whether, as was suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) yesterday, by a supply bill, or in the same manner that I have indicated, namely, by extending the provisions of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act of 1931 for a further period of two months up until the first of May. Now, so far as a supply bill is concerned, I think it is fairly obvious to those who have followed me that to ask for any particular sum of money at this time in the form of a supply bill with the usual limitations that are imposed upon such measures would not meet the situation. In our judgment at any rate, having regard to our experience, it would not. Parliament is in session, parliament has the fullest opportunity to consider and criticize and deal with every step the administration takes. I am not lacking either in sympathy or respect for the views that were so strongiy urged last session, and doubtless will be again urged, against our taking the course which I am asking the house to permit us to take, namely, to declare that the provisions of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act of 1931 shall continue for a further period of two months. I do that, you may say, with some reluctance, but I do it because I believe it is the only method having regard to the neces-

Unemployment Continuance Act
s;ty for elastic provisions to deal with complex problems promptly. But I do sympathize with the views expressed in a few words yesterday by the right hon. leader of the opposition, and so I suggest to this house that we frame and add to the single section of the bill which makes the provisions of the statute of 1931 applicable for another two months, a provision whereby every order in council that is approved by the Governor General shall be laid upon the table of this house at the next sitting following its passing. That, of course, would be the next day, if the house were in session. I cannot but think, having regard to the gravity of the situation and the difficulty of dealing with it by any hard and fast rule, that this chamber will confer these powers upon this government. I would not deprive this parliament of its right to criticize freely and, if it thought desirable, destroy this administration for the improper discharge of its obligations, but I can conceive of no way in which this house can have larger powers conferred upon it than by the method I have suggested, so that in every instance it might have the fullest opportunity of dealing with these matters.
The answer is, of course, that it is done before the opportunity is afforded to criticize.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, sir, I can only
record my own experience since August last in dealing with this matter, and I do say frankly to this chamber that I know of no way by which you can deal with this difficult problem unless you have the widest discretion in an administrative sense. After all, it is a problem of administration, and I know of no method by which you could deal with these problems as problems of administration unless you have the powers I have indicated.
I will give an illustration. Last j'ear we took power to deal with peace, order and good government. In the fall it became apparent that it was vitally important that we should make our practice uniform with that of the United States with respect to the valuation of securities held by insurance companies. Many of the United States companies were doing business in Canada and many of our Canadian companies were doing business in that country. Forty-eight superintendents of insurance got together, and forty-seven of them agreed that for the purposes of valuation, the conditions being so exceptional, the average value for the last five quarters should be the governing valuation for certain classes of securities. Unless that power had been conferred upon us by this statute we could 
not have enacted the order in council, which was published in the Gazette and which all hon. members of this house no doubt have seen.

Are you
sure you are right in that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am perfectly certain
that no one will question the fact that when you begin to deal with hundreds of millions of dollars, and when you remember that it is not the values of to-day that concern the policyholders but the values in future, based upon what money will earn and what it is necessary to set aside for the purpose of meeting liabilities in the future, to place a value based upon the average value for the last five quarters, as they did, with our companies doing business in the United States and their companies doing business here, was but to say that there should be some measure of certainty and uniformity in fixing values in the most important matter with which we as a government had to deal at the moment. We must remember the magnitude of the sums involved, and the fact that the happiness of the people may be in some sense disturbed by any condition arising that would bring about a disturbance of the stable foundations on which these institutions have been built Unless we had possessed that power we could not have passed that order in council.
Now I put it to the house whether or not there is an element of grave risk if such a power, is not vested in the executive at a time of great flux and change in the economic conditions of a country. The possibilities of abuse are always present in the minds of a parliament-

Just one question. Apart from this order in council respecting the Insurance Act, which virtually amended that statute, were there any orders in council passed under that peace, order and good government provision of the statute of last year, amending other acts of parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As far as orders in
council amending acts of parliament are concerned, I have nothing in mind at the moment. There may be something of which I cannot think just now, but all the orders in council will be laid on the table at an early date, and an opportunity will be afforded for the discussion of them. The reasons, of course, for the particular order in council to which I referred, which was published in the Gazette and which no doubt the hon. gentleman has read, were not only the conditions to which I have referred but also a judgment of the

Unemployment Continuance Act
privy council which was delivered in October, and also the necessity for providing uniformity.
Let me put it this way: If an insurance company has a mortgage, it is still regarded as an asset at its face value, as a mortgage. However, with shares and bonds, the value fixed is the average value for the last five quarters, which was considered fair by the insurance superintendents to whom I have referred. There are other matters that arise from time to time. What we seek by this resolution is authority from this house to continue until the first day of May the provisions of the statute which was enacted last session. It confers a wide discretion upon the executive; I said so last year, and I repeat it now. I am not one of those who do not understand and appreciate the attitude of mind taken by the opposition with respect to this question, but I do say with some degree of pride and satisfaction that although that statute came into force in August and we have administered it ever since, you will have great difficulty and indeed I think you will find it impossible, sir, to point to any case in which there has been an abuse of authority under it or where there has not been an honest administration of its provisions. That I believe I can safely say.

The right hon. gentleman referred to the $6,000,000 for feed and seed in Saskatchewan. Has he made any estimate of the money which will be required to provide relief for the unemployed and the distressed in this dried out area until they get a crop, which will be about September 1 next? If so, could the Prime Minister give us the amount of the estimate, and tell us whether provisions have been made to look after these people?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a most difficult thing to do; it depends so much upon the season, the production of vegetables and so many other things which my hon. friend, living in a part of that area, knows as well as I know. The government and the commission are unable to express, in terms of dollars, their view at the moment of what may be required, although they believe that with the opening of spring they will be able to do so, and I trust that between now and May I may be able to give this house a fairly reasonable and intelligent estimate of the position. I think the hon. gentleman knows quite as well as I do, if not better, how difficult it would be at this time to give that estimate in dollars and cents.
What is to be the policy of the government with regard to provinces other than Saskatchewan after May 1?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not a question which at this time I can answer; that must be dealt with later. There was one other matter which I am reminded was dealt with by order in council; that was the question of the export of gold. I thought perhaps that was well known to all hon. members of the house, but that is another case. It was mentioned the other day in answer to a question. The passing of an order in council prohibiting the export of gold except under licence was done under the provisions of the statute. That occurs to me as I pass on, and that became very essential for reasons I think I made quite clear to the house the other evening.
I cannot, Mr. Speaker, usefully add more to the explanation which I felt it incumbent upon me to make to this house in asking that you do now leave the chair that the committee may consider this resolution. I am reluctant, in the constitutional sense, to ask for the continuance of these powers; I am not reluctant on any other ground. And if I knew of any other method which I believed would accomplish the end we have in view, of assisting in the fair discharge of our obligations, I would not ask this. But after the most careful thought that I have been able to give to the subject-and I will welcome any suggestions that others may offer towards the solution of the problem- I know of no way, except by this method, whereby we can assist the provinces and supplement the work they have to undertake, and at the same time have ready at all times the executive power which would enable us, if the occasion arose, to deal with the situation on a competent basis. It is for that reason that I commend this resolution to the favourable consideration of the house, realizing that I have taken much longer time presenting these various matters to the chamber than I had expected, but realizing also that the house required of us some account of our stewardship in the discharge of the great responsibilities that rested upon us in view of the wide discretion and the great powers which were committed into our hands.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am sure the
house and the country will appreciate the lucid and comprehensive statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has just made of what he very rightly terms the stewardship of the government in its administration of the

Unemployment Continuance Act
statute of this parliament respecting unemployment and farm relief. I could not help feeling, as my right hon. friend spoke, that the responsibilities of office are having a wholesome and chastening effect upon him, and that he is beginning to realize that, in many courses of action which have been taken in the past, he would have been wiser had he then entertained and espoused with the zeal he has done to-day the views he has expressed to the house this afternoon. May I say that, with most of what my right hon. friend has said by way of exposition I have no exception whatever to take. I can only regret that when he occupied the position of leader of the opposition and the government of the day was seeking to defend the treasury, as he today is seeking to defend it, he did not then join with us in expressing agreement in the view we then put forward as to the respective responsibilities of the municipalities, the provinces and the Dominion, for those views were precisely the same as the views which to-day he says the present government entertains.
May I also express regret that during the period of the general election, when my right hon. friend was appealing to the electorate, and particularly when he was dealing with this all important question of unemployment relief, he did not then put forward, as the government of the day put forward, the view of the respective relationships and obligations of the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities, in the way in which he has stated them this afternoon. I might go further, and say that I regret that at the special session of parliament, and at the last session as well, when we were presenting some of the points of view which he has presented with 6uch force and eloquence to-day, my right hon. friend did not at that time accept the view we were urging upon the government. Had he done so, the country to-day would be in a very different position, and the federal treasury would have to its credit an amount very considerably more than it has at the present time.
My right hon. friend opened his address by enlarging upon the jurisdiction of the dominion and the provinces respectively in the matter of unemployment relief. He cited from decisions of the privy council as rendered by the late Lord Haldane in the board of commerce case, and in the case of newsprint prices, each of which judgments was mentioned in order to emphasize the point which the right hon. gentleman was seeking to drive home, namely, that with respect to matters of unemployment relief the obligation in the first instance was 
a provincial obligation, and that, so far as the federal government was concerned, its part in the matter was that of supplementing the provinces and coming to their aid, only when the provinces themselves were unable to cope with the situation. May I remind the house that this was the position which we, as a Liberal party, when in office, took from the outset. It was the position we took during the period of the campaign. And it is the position we have taken since we have been on this side of the house. If there has been a different position taken, if my right hon. friend has stressed the point that the emergency has been of a national character, bo great as to necessitate the exercise of powers by the federal government much wider than would otherwise have been the case, he himself has been the one to put forward that point of view and to press it to the extreme he has. I want to make quite clear that at last, after dealing with this problem of unemployment relief for a year and a half, my right hon. friend now states a position which he asks us to support, in direct opposition to the view as stated by him when he was on this side of the house, during the general elections, and when he first came into power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I hope my right hon.
friend will not think I am interrupting him, but the language I used a year ago I have in front of me, exactly as I used to-day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Those who
have heard my right hon. friend will have no difficulty in seeing the accuracy of what I have said as to his presentations. Indeed, as my right hon. friend was reading the judgment of Lord Haldane, and when, in particular, he emphasized the point that the federal jurisdiction overrode that of the provinces only in a time of emergency in .the nature of war, I was somewhat surprised that it did not occur to his mind at that moment that with respect to the statute passed at the last session of parliament, we on this side of the house urged that very reason as one why the enactment should not be adapted. We pointed out that the statute passed at the last session, giving to the government powers to deal by order in council with peace, order and good government, was one which could be justified only in time of war, insurrection, invasion and that as a matter of fact, even in time of actual war, the government of Sir Robert Borden had never sought to obtain from this parliament powers as extreme as those which the right hon. gentleman asks that this parliament should enact. To-day he is asking us to reenact the very statute

Unemployment Continuance Act
to which we took exception in such strong terms at the last session of parliament. I say to my right hon. friend that, when he asks us to-day to reenact the statute passed at the last session, we must confront him with the argument which he himself has presented this afternoon as one against taking that particular course. There does not exist at the present time an emergency equivalent to that of actual or threatened invasion or war. There does not exist the condition which, according to the judgment of Lord Haldane, is the only one which would justify giving to the government the powers which the Prime Minister is asking under this particular act. So much for the first part of my right hon. friend's remarks.
May I say to my right hon. friend that when he was speaking to the public of this country about the cries of little children, about what he termed the smug complacency of the then Prime Minister who he said was deaf to the cries to heal their pain, which were being made to my right hon. friend as a Canadian and as a Christian, he was not stressing, as he has done to-day, the jurisdiction as between the provinces and the dominion in the matter of unemployment relief. Being in power to-day, instead of making his appeal to the human needs and aspects of the situation, he gives as consolation to the hungry and starving two judgments of the late Lord Haldane.
I come now to the next point with which my right hon. friend dealt. He spoke of the loans which this government has made to the provinces since September last. In dealing with that point, he said that the government's action was based on the alternative of either making loans to the provinces or of allowing the provinces to default in their obligations. He asked the house whether the government was not in the right in making the loans, instead of permitting the provinces to default. I say to my right hon. friend that if, before making the commitments which he has made with respect to the expenditure of public moneys, he had accepted the suggestion made from this side of the house at the special session, and again with particular emphasis at the last session of parliament, and had called a conference of the dominion and the provinces to discuss their financial relations, he might not have been obliged to make the loans he has made during the last few months, and he certainly would not have been obliged to make them to the extent to which they have been made.
My right hon. friend must surely recall that when he and his colleagues were introducing measures to provide for the voting of large sums for unemployment relief and for the reenactment of grants in aid to the provinces for technical education; when they were introducing legislation with respect to old age pensions, construction of highways, and other matters, we on this side urged strongly that before making commitments which involved so considerable a drain on the federal treasury, the government call the provinces into conference and discuss with them the whole financial situation of the provinces and the dominion. Hon. gentlemen opposite must remember that, because it was very strongly stressed from this side. If that suggestion had been followed, if that course had been adopted, the situation to-day would be very different from what it is. I think it is an open secret that, in dealing with the provinces, my right hon. friend told the premiers or provincial treasurers that, with respect to expenditures which they were making, he in control of the federal treasury and of the government of Canada would not countenance loans to them beyond a certain point unless they discontinued some of their expenditures and curtailed in many ways the outlays of public money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think that is
correct; I recall no occasion on which that was so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If it is to be understood that provinces like British Columbia are to be free to spend public money in any way they please and are, notwithstanding, to get all they want in the way of loans from this parliament, then we are embarking upon an expenditure of public moneys which is wholly indefensible. If the course I suggested has not been taken, it should be taken, and the provinces given to understand that, if their expenditures are unwise or injudicious, they must be curtailed if they expect to have their revenues supplemented by loans from the federal treasury to meet an emergent situation.
My right hon. friend spoke, next, of the province of Saskatchewan, and he dealt with what he described as the admirable manner in which relief had been administered in that province. He stressed the splendid service which had been given by the unemployment relief commission, and he drew the attention of the house to the fact that the federal government made its contribution to the province by means of a cheque payable to the unemployment relief commission. He stated that this commission had carried out the work of unemployment relief in cooperation with the province and the municipalities, and in addition to what was being achieved by voluntary co-
operation, and that it had used all the safeguards it could in the matter of protecting public expenditure.
If an unemployment relief commission has worked so successfully in one province in connection with the expenditure of public moneys for relief, why has not my right hon. friend adopted, before this, the suggestion which has been made over and over again from this side of the house of having an unemployment relief commission deal after the same manner with dominion unemployment relief? Instead of giving to the governor in council the power to spend money at its will without consultation even with parliament, why are we not doing what was done in Saskatchewan, particularly when, as the Prime Minister says it has, the example has so much to commend it? I say to my right hon. friend that even now he should adopt that course, notwithstanding the fact that he has not adopted it up to the present time.
With the example of Saskatchewan before him, instead of coming and asking this parliament to give to the government the power, by order in council, to grant unemployment relief and relief for distress in rural areas, my right hon. friend should establish immediately an unemployment relief commission, composed, as I stated the other day, of representatives of the different economic interests involved. This commission should be given the power to do what may be necessary and this parliament should make its cheque payable, through the executive, to the relief commission, which body would transmit to parliament a full statement of the manner in which the money has been expended. I say that it is no longer defensible to ask parliament to vote further sums to the governor in council when, out of the lips of the Prime Minister himself, we have the declaration that unemployment relief has been better administered under a relief commission in Saskatchewan than has been the case elsewhere.
I stress that again, and in speaking of it, may I point out another feature? It seems to me most unfortunate and indeed lamentable that, after having spent millions of dollars, as the federal government has done, upon unemployment relief, as a result of the legislation of the special session and also that of last session, we have nothing at all in the way of accumulated information which can be put at the disposal of parliament to guide us in regard to this great subject of unemployment relief.
If a 'commission of the character which I have mentioned had been appointed over a year and a half ago, or when the government

Unemployment Continuance Act
came into office, that commission, if composed of the right personnel, as it might well have been, would to-day have 'bad a fund of information which it could place before a committee of parliament with respect to the whole problem of unemployment relief, information the like of which could not have been obtained in any other way. A commission of that character would have been in a better position than any other body to advise parliament as to the considerations of which account should be taken in the enactment of a compulsory unemployment insurance measure. But, while we have spent our millions of dollars, we have practically nothing to show for them, except the report which will be brought down indicating the total amount of expenditure, the total addition thereby to the public debt, and the way in which it was made. It is not, however, yet too late to do something that will be helpful to parliament and to the country in the way of acquiring that special information and knowledge, which should be gathered for the use of parliament at subsequent sessions, and which at the same time will safeguard further expenditures in a manner which, according to the Prime Minister's own statement this afternoon, is the best of all.
Those, I think, were the main points to which my right hon. friend referred, until he caime to the concluding portion of his address. There he indicated the problem with which the government is at the moment confronted. It is the same problem that confronted the government at the special session. It is the same problem which confronted the government at the last session. The only difference is that we have had now an experience of a year and a half which we had not at the outset, and that experience certainly ought to guide us with respect to action which should hereafter be taken. My right hon. friend was quick to recognize that there are very strong reasons why, with parliament in session, there should not be given to the governor in council power which might, with plausible excuse or reason, be asked for in times when parliament is not in session. I wish to speak with particular reference to that aspect for I do not like to witness the gradual elimination of the duties and functions of the Commons, one might almost say, the disappearance of parliament itself through the surrender of its rights and responsibilities to the executive and a parting with their control over expenditures on the part of the people's representatives in this house.
But, before I go into that, the most important phase, may I say a word or two about the measure which is now before the house. The motion is:
That the house go into committee of the whole to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
Chapter 58 of the statutes of 1931 is an act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemployment and farm relief, and the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada. The section to be amended is section 8, which reads:
This act shall expire on the first day of March, 1932.
As I pointed out the other day, this act expired on the first day of March, 1932. When I spoke last on this measure, it was the first day of March, and I was prepared to leave it an open question as to whether the act would expire at midnight of that day or whether it had expired at midnight of the previous day. I think the latter view is the correct one, hut, at any rate, there can now be no question about the act having expired. Therefore, chapter 58 of the Statutes of Canada, 1931, which we are now being asked to amend, no longer exists. That statute is as dead as a door marl. How can parliament be asked to amend a statute which does not exist? How can we be asked to amend an extinct, a dead, a defunct statute? Parliament can revive a statute; it is possible for the ministry to bring in a bill reenacting an old statute, but, in the form in which it is now before the house, the resolution is asking parliament to do something which it is impossible for any parliament on earth to do.
It is not befitting the dignity of parliament, it is a contempt of parliament that it should be asked to amend a statute which no longer exists, and I wish to state at once that we on this side must take very strong exception to the House of Commons attempting to proceed in any such way. After all, we have responsibilities in the matter of the precedents which we set in this parliament. Surely my right hon. friend is not going to associate his name with a precedent that will mean that, hereafter, any hon. member will be wholly in order if he brings jn a bill to amend some statute that is no longer in existence, some enactment that has disappeared into the limbo of forgotten and abandoned things. If we have power to amend this statute, which was passed last session and which expired on the first day of March, any hon. member can, with propriety, introduce into the house a bill to amend any enactment that has been passed by this parliament at any time since it came into being. When the commissioners revise



Unemployment Continuance Act
the statutes and discard old enactments that have ceased to exist, they are at least supposed to be serving a useful public purpose, namely to keep, in a form which will be readily accessible, those enactments which are alive, which still have the force of law. But this statute has no longer the force of law. It is, as I have said, no longer in existence. I protest against the introduction of this resolution, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will take the position, as the presiding officer of the house, that in the form in which it is presented it cannot be entertained.
In saying that, let me make this perfectly clear. I am not raising this objection as a merely technical one. I am raising it, as I have said, because I feel that the precedents which are established in this house are allimportant, and that members of the House of Commons incur a very grave responsibility in countenancing precedents which should not be set. To make clear that this exception is not being taken on merely technical grounds; that we are not trying to obstruct the voting of any moneys which may be necessary in order to give the provinces the needed loans that my right hon. friend says he now proposes to give them, let me say again as I said yesterday: If my right hon. friend will drop the resolution which is now before us and ask his Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) to come to the house this evening with a supply bill indicating the amount of money which the administration feels it will be necessary to have in order to meet the situation between now and the first of May, or the period during which parliament may be in session, if he will take that course, and move that the rules be suspended so that such a supply bill can be speedily passed through the house and sent over to the Senate, we of the opposition will cordially join with the government in agreeing to the suspension of the rules, and will seek to expedite the passage of such a measure through the house to-day. I make an urgent appeal to my right hon. friend,-who as Prime Minister surely has an appreciation of the responsibility involved in the setting of a precedent, who surely venerates British parliamentary institutions and would like to have them upheld- I appeal to him at this time not to be responsible for a controversy in this house over the method of doing something which all of us, regardless of the parties to which we belong, are prepared to assist the government in doing and say should be done, particularly when that controversy relates only to the taking of a right course, and the avoidance of a course which hitherto has not been taken 
in this parliament, and cannot be countenanced under constitutional practice and procedure, as we have sought to uphold them.
I know my right hon. friend has power through parliament to revive a dead statute; he can bring in a bill to provide that a certain enactment, known as chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, be reenacted. I say that that course will have to be taken before he can obtain the relief he seeks. Relief cannot be obtained under the terms of the resolution before us. Again I urge the ministry not to create a controversy, particularly when delay might only serve to cause added suffering to many people throughout 'the west and in other parts of Canada. There need be no delay whatever. As I have said we can expedite a supply bill to the extent of having it pass this House of Commons to-day, if the ministry wishes to proceed with it in the regular manner in which all supply is granted by parliament.
Moneys required for purposes of unemployment and farm relief should be voted in a manner similar to the regular votes of supply in the House of Commons. May I compare the resplution now before us with the resolutions of the two previous years which have preceded bills for the purpose of securing from parliament relief for the unemployed. The first measure of the government opposite with respect to unemployment relief, and which had to do with the granting of public moneys, was preceded by the following resolution introduced in this house on September 10, 1930, during the special session:
That it is expedient to provide that a sum not exceeding twenty million dollars be appropriated and paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for the relief of unemployment in constructing, extending or improving public works and undertakings, railways, highways, etc., that will assist in providing useful and suitable work for the unemployed, all as set forth in a bill founded on this resolution.
At that time hon. members on this side of the house took exception to the government proceeding by waj' of a special bill rather than by the customary way of bringing in a supply bill. We drew attention to the fact that the House of Commons should exercise control over expenditures, and, if a supply bill were brought in, a certain amount of money would be voted for use until the beginning of the new fiscal year. Had a supply bill been introduced, the government would have been in a position to meet all its obligations. At that time we urged the government, in the expenditure of large sums of public money, not to depart from the long established practice of proceeding in the regular way through a supply bill. We also
