drew attention to the fact that, according to the practices of parliament, not only should the expenditure of the amount named be confined to the fiscal year, but the specific purposes for which the moneys were required should be set out. Had the government voted a sum necessary or sufficient for the period of time for which it was required, pending the regular session of parliament the amount named at -the outset would never have been permitted to assume the proportions set forth in the bill. There never would have been a suggestion of $20,000,000, but, as I said the other day, the amount required would have been about $4,000,000.
Having secured this vast sum of $20,000,000, the government when it came to parliament again found it very difficult to name any sum which would be required, and for that reason they went further than they had previously gone and asked us to vote a blank cheque. The first resolution was a departure from the practice of parliament, in that the amount required was not voted as supply is ordinarily voted, for the period only of the fiscal year or part of a fiscal year. Having obtained the $20,000,000 the government made commitments with respect to the greater proportion of that money for expenditures, not in the last part of the fiscal year 1930-1931, but for the next fiscal year. Those commitments led to the expenditure of millions of dollars which otherwise would never have been spent. My right hon. friend takes pride in these actions of his government. I say, that they wasted public moneys through the manner in which they made commitments for its expenditure during the spring, summer and fall months. Those expenditures would never have been what they were had the government followed the customary procedure of asking parliament, the peoples representatives assembled, for the amount required for the fiscal year, and for that period alone. Having made that mistake twice, do not let us repeat it a third time.
At the time the government took that course, we pointed out that, if parliament once departed from constitutional procedure, one could never tell to what lengths such departures might lead. Our representations at that time proved to be true with respect to the measure brought in at the following session. At this point, I shall read the resolution introduced at that time, and ask hon. members to contrast it with the one to which I referred a few moments ago. The first one named a specific sum of money, specific objects or works upon which this money was to be spent At least it had that virtue. The next year, however, what there was of virtue in that 41761-58J
regard in the first resolution was entirely lacking in the second and in the bill based upon it.
The resolution introduced on July 27, 1931, was as follows:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to employment and farm relief; and for the maintenance and peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada; and to authorize the governor in council to expend for the said purposes out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may from time to time be necessary.
Here was a resolution which went very much farther than the original resolution. The first unemployment legislation enabled the government to make commitments beyond the fiscal year; in that particular it was bad enough. The measure I have just read, however, gave the government power to spend any sum it pleased, and, to all intents and purposes, it substituted the executive for parliament during the period of time to which it applied. It took out of the hands of parliament altogether the control of the public moneys that were being spent. Now, that is a very serious thing. Let me repeat: the second measure took from parliament altogether, from the time that parliament ceased to be in session to the time of its reassembling this year, all control of public expenditures with respect to anything that might be said to have to do with unemployment relief and with the relief of distress. That was an extreme step, a step, I think, the like of which has never been taken in this or any other parliament.
But what is now being proposed? That step was defended a year ago on the score that parliament was then about to prorogue, that the unemployment situation would exist throughout the winter, that the government must be given a free hand to deal with it. Parliament was not in the mood, nor, had it the time when the measure was introduced, to consider as carefully as it should have the consequences of a step of the kind. But parliament is in session now, and we are being asked to do, for the period of time that parliament itself is in session, something to which we took exception with respect to the period during which parliament would not be in session at all. I say, Mr. Speaker, there can be no excuse for any action of that kind. We might as well abandon parliament altogether. Why are we assembled here if while the people's representatives are in session the ministry is to get power to do, by order in council, anything it pleases?
Stop for a moment, and look at the bill more closely. It asks that this power be given for the months of March and April;

Unemployment Continuance Act
that is, up until the first of May. I assume this parliament is going to continue in session at any rate until the first of May. I have my suspicions whether the government has not in mind the adjournment of parliament on the first of May, if we are not in a position to prorogue at that time. I repeat, parliament is now in session. Why should any power be given to the government to do by order in council what can be done in the regular way by parliamentary enactment? We cannot permit a step of that kind to be taken, if it is at all possible to prevent it. We do not wish to obstruct the government in any legislation they may have in mind. We do not wish to add an hour's delay to their obtaining any sum of money that they may consider necessary to meet existing needs; but we cannot countenance a step which means giving the government power to do by order in council, while parliament is in session, the thing which parliament itself alone should do. It is an indignity to parliament itself that any such power should be asked for.
Contempt.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Why should
members of parliament assemble here at all, unless it be amongst other things to exercise some control over the expenditure of public moneys? That is the fundamental basis of everything we hold dear in the way of responsible government. We cannot jettison the whole institution of responsible government just because the Prime Minister says it is going to be difficult for him to make up his mind what amount of money is needed.
My right hon. friend says there never was a problem as great as the problem with which Canada was faced last year. As I have pointed out, my right hon. friend has a way of saying, as well as doing, the extreme thing. Surely the problems with which this country was confronted during the period of the war-*

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We never had 100,000
people hungry.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My right hon. friend still holds the view that the problems confronting his government are greater than the problems which Sir Robert Borden had to contend with during the period of war. I can never entertain that view, nor do I think any hon. members on the other side will ever agree with their leader in that respect. But Sir Robert Borden never asked parliament to do what the Prime Minister at the present moment is asking parliament to do. Sir Robert Borden asked parliament to vote, year by year, what was needed to maintain the armies at the front and to meet all the expenditures

that were essential in connection with the war. He called a special session of parliament in order to obtain in a regular way the money that he required. He did not at that session ask that the House of Commons should give his cabinet power to pay out of the treasury what moneys they might consider necessary during the next few months or during the period of the war. He named the required amount. He was perfectly frank in saying: This amount may not be sufficient. It may be too large or it may not be large enough; but, if it is not large enough, I will bring parliament back, and I will obtain authority for further expenditures. Now, my right hon. friend has parliament in session. He does not need to summon parliament again to get an additional sum for the purposes for which he now requires this money. He has indicated this afternoon that something like, I think, $7,000,000 will be required for the purpose of loans. Well, let him ask for $7,000,000 for the purpose mentioned and we will vote it. If, between now and the first of May, he finds $7,000,000 will not be sufficient, let him come back and tell us it is not sufficient and say what additional sum he requires. But I submit he has no right, while we are assembled here, to ask for a blank cheque to do as he pleases by order in council.
But the act he desires us to reenact goes very much further than the voting of public money. Look for a moment at the act, the provisions of which we are being asked to renew at the present time. There are really three distinct measures in one in this enactment. I pointed that out last session when the government was asking us to pass it. There is a measure for unemployment relief. There is also a measure for farm relief, and a measure to confer on the government certain powers with respect to the "peace, order and good government of Canada." At the time, we took exception to these three distinct measures being passed as one. However, they were passed. But now, while parliament is in session, we are again being asked to give to the government three separate enactments in one for this period of time. I think my right hon. friend can hardly have considered the real significance of the action he is asking parliament at the moment to take.
With respect to the "peace, order and good government" clauses of this enactment, last session, I drew attention to the fact that the language was taken from legislation passed during the period of the war, that it was the language of the War Measures Act, which conferred very wide powers upon the government. But I drew attention to the further fact that the enactment, which originally conferred those wide powers on the government

Unemployment Continuance Act
of the day, made it very clear that those powers could only be exercised in case of actual war or invasion, or insurrection, real or apprehended, and that they could not be exercised at any other time or for any other reason. Last session my right hon. friend secured from parliament the right to exercise at will, during the time parliament was not in session, those powers which heretofore had never been exercised except during a period of war, insurrection and invasion. Now he comes to ask us to allow him to exercise them while parliament itself is in session. I say, Mr. Speaker, that we, as members of the House of Commons, responsible to the people of this country, cannot surrender every obligation that is imposed upon us to protect their rights. My right hon. friend read from Lord Haldane's judgment paragraph after paragraph which asserted that, even with respect to such a comparatively small matter as that of over. riding the jurisdiction of a province in certain particulars, it could not be done by the government except at a time of actual war or of an emergent situation that was so grave as to make it appear that war was already upon us. At the time I took down the words quoted by my right hon. friend from the judgment of Lord Haldane, and they were "a sufficiently great emergency such as that arising out of war." That was the only occasion mentioned.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend read two judgments; at any rate whether it was war or war-famine; both have to do with war or with situations arising out of war. I do submit, Mr. Speaker, even if it might 'be necessary for anry reason to give the government of the day power to deal with certain matters by order in council when parliament is not in session and when it might necessitate a delay of a month or more before action could be taken by parliament, there can be no excuse whatever for conferring that power upon the government while the representatives of the people surround the ministers of the crown in parliament assembled. So I say to my right hon. friend that we must strenuously oppose the legislation in the form in which he is seeking to introduce it.	*
May I briefly summarize our position, as I have endeavoured to state it. With the object which the government has in view, namely supplying public moneys for purposes of relief, we are in complete accord and agreement. We are ready to leave to the judgment of the ministry itself the amount it may need for the purpose of dealing with unemployment relief, the supplying of seed or the meeting of any other need which would come within the provisions of the legislation proposed. All that we ask is that the ministry bring in a supply bill indicating the amount they wish to have for the general purposes, and allow us to vote the required amounts in that form. We take exception to the course the ministry seeks to follow, first of all because it asks us to do something which is impossible. I am going to appeal to you if need be, Mr. Speaker, to give your ruling on that point: to decide whether or not the resolution which is before the house is one which this house can entertain, asking us as it does to amend a dead enactment. I say we cannot do it; we should not be asked to do it; and it is an indignity to be asked to do it. But, assuming that the government should get around that difficulty by introducing some other resolution which will revive this dead enactment, assuming they do so and then ask us to amend it, we will have to take exception to doing so for the reason I have mentioned-that it overrides the customary procedure and that there is no necessity therefor, since parliament is here assembled and at a moment's notice can, if what is suggested is right and proper, do anything the ministry wishes it to do.
My right hon. friend says he will lay on the table of the house the orders in council that are passed the day after they are passed. We want to know the contents of an order in council, not the day after it has been passed, but the day before it is passed, and the representatives of the people have a right to such knowledge. If my right hon. friend thinks it is necessary to have money for some particular purpose, let him come to this house and ask for supply for the required purpose and give us a chance to discuss the matter. If we approve of the measure proposed we will pass it, but we cannot surrender the right to control public expenditure, and we cannot pass over all the powers, the dignities, the rights, and the responsibilities of the House of Commons to an executive which wishes to place itself wholly beyond the control of this legislative body.

No, I said just the

Mr. Speaker, in the debate on this resolution I submit to hon. members that everything in connection with the whole history of unemployment and farm relief is open for discussion. I think hon. members will find in the resolution now before us, innocent looking though it is, more objectionable features than Were to be found in the monstrosity of last session which passed under the caption of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act.
In effect, the suggestion now is made that we should reenact the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act as from the date the bill to be founded on the proposed resolution becomes law, namely when it receives the assent of His Excellency the Governor General. Hon. members will have to consider whether, after the experience they have had in the last year, they are content in effect to put upon the statute books of the session of 1932 an act in the terms of the unemployment and farm relief act of last year but expiring on the first of May next.
In the year 1930 the need, as it was represented throughout the country, was for relief and adequate measures to deal with and to remedy unemployment. Everywhere on the hustings and at various meetings addressed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) promises were made that unemployment would be ended. No suggestion was given at that time that there could be any doubt about it; no qualifications were attached ini any way. The statement was made that unemployment would cease and that work would be available for all who were willing to work.
When at the special session of 1930, however we came to consider the medium through which this relief was to be accomplished, we were met with a proposal, not carefully considered and capable of meeting the situation having regard to the various avocations to be considered, but comprised in a bare, bald provision to the effect that there should be contributed out of the consolidated revenue of Canada the sum of $20,000,000 for unemployment relief. Owing to the fact that the present Prime Minister wanted to go immediately to attend meetings of the Imperial economic conference, parliament passed the measure. At the same time amendments were made to the tariff changing not only the schedules but giving to the governor in council many of the powers of parliament with regard to the valuation of goods for duty purposes.
Winter passed; unemployment was not relieved, but became greater than before; so
that in the session of 1931 we were met with a proposal that measures for unemployment relief should be given a new lease of life, and that the bill which the government is now attempting to resurrect, and which was to enable the Prime Minister to carry out his pledges, should be passed. That bill was passed-a bill giving to hon. members occupying the treasury benches all the powers of parliament, so far as the exercise of legislative and administrative jurisdiction was concerned, and containing no limit as to the amount which might be spent. In other words, the powers of parliament and the unlimited resources of the treasury of Canada were taken into the hands and keeping of the cabinet. During the .past year that act has been in operation. One might have expected that during that time the government would have gained sufficient experience to enable it at this time to come before the country and make a proposal which would deal in a businesslike way, with our unemployment situation. Instead of that however we have before us what at first sight would appear to be an innocent resolution, an innocent amendment, reminding one of the old game we used to play at school, but instead of rubbing out "x" and putting in "o" we are now rubbing out "March" and putting in "May". The purpose of the bill is to vest in the members of the government of Canada until the first of May those wide powers to which I have referred. One might have imagined the government would have realized that a large number of people in Canada have only the commodity of labour for sale, and that in some way or other, with its vast powers and the ability it is supposed to possess, the government would have made it possible for those labouring men to dispose of that commodity in exchange for wages.
When the right hon. gentleman was sitting on this side of the house I have heard him make statements constituting not a suggestion of policy, nothing definite as to what he would do, but consisting for the most part of this phrase repeated over and over again: "Statemanship is not so barren but what a solution can be found for any problem which presents itself." At other times when my right hon. friend was asked what his policy was he has quoted those words of Gladstone of which he seems to be so fond.: "When I am called in I will prescribe." He has been called in. An opportunity has been given to him to prepare the prescription. In this year of grace 1932, after sixteen months trial of makeshift legislation, at a time when the life of a bill is about to expire, there is put on the order paper of this house a suggestion

Unemployment Continuance Act
that such bill be renewed for a period of two months. What does it mean? The meaning is that my hon, friends opposite have not been able to work out a solution for the problem; it is a confession of defeat and an admission that they do not know what to do. Like Micawber they hoped that something would turn up, that times would get better and that unemployment might decrease. But conditions did not inprove; from day to day they became worse, and finally one day in council meeting someone said: "The Unemployment and Farm Relief Act is running out; what will we do about unemployment?"-and the casual answer was "Oh, well, let us extend the old act for a couple of months." That is the policy which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and his cabinet bring before the country at this time. After the promises which have been made, after the undertakings which have been given, after the support which has been received, after having had a comfortable majority on that side of the house in order to work their will and do whatever they wish, yes, and with the whole power of parliament in their hands, they have to confess: The best we can do is to renew the note for a couple of months in the hope that something will turn up.

And they are late
at that.

And as my hon. friend
remarks, before the renewal comes the note is overdue. One would have thought that when this session was called early in February, and the figures showed that unemployment was even worse than it had been-I am sorry to say-when that situation appeared one would have thought that the very first piece of legislation to be put on the order paper by the government would be something in connection with unemployment. What do we find? The Juvenile Delinquents Act has to be amended and that is trotted out, the Destructive Insect and Pest Act has to be passed through all its stages, and investigations have to be launched about this, that and the other thing because somebody happened to make faces at somebody else; all these things are dealt with, but no action is taken with respect to the vital question of unemployment until February 26, three days before the act ran out-at that they had to count on leap year, and then this resolution is put on the order paper. Its purpose, as I said before, is simply to scratch out "March" and put in "May." Possibly by that time parliament may be prorogued. But that is the way the unemployment problem has been

dealt with by the government. Some member of 'the government woke up to the fact that they were pretty nearly at the end of the month and made the bright and original suggestion:	We will run the act along until
the first of May.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the act itself, because having had this experience the government knows what that legislation has enabled them to accomplish. Judged by the test of experience I submit that the legislation has proved to be pitiably inadequate and futile as a practical measure to relieve unemployment. I submit further that the cost has been extravagant and the expenditure wasteful. I submit; thirdly, that, due to lack of proper supervision, in many cases the relief has not reached those for whom it was intended.
Let me deal first with the results accomplished in the way of providing practical employment. The only statement we have is that which was made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) on February 23rd in connection with the debate on the amendment by the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) to a motion that your honour leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply. This afternoon the Prime Minister in proposing the resolution gave us a comprehensive and lucid statement, as it was quite properly characterized by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), with regard to the operation of the act. But after all this was only a general outline, and even yet we have not been advised what the government knows with regard to the actual experience and the details of its administration. The only information given to us is to be found in the figures which were furnished by the Minister of Labour a couple of weeks ago in which he told the house that there was spent in 1930 870,472,832, of which the federal government's share was 817,372,848; and that in 1931 the aggregate expenditure was 876,426,387, of which the federal authorities spent 832,822,847.

I find it very difficult to deal with the matter, Mr. Speaker. I shall have to deal with it on the figures furnished by the Minister of Labour and as they appear in the Labour Gazette; then my right hon. friend and his colleagues can point out any inaccuracies in my calculations. I think the Minister of Labour did say the amount had been spent, and I take it the labour had been performed, but possibly cheques had not been issued. The difficulty is to find what was spent and what employment was provided. If you look at the Labour Gazette of September 31, you will find that up to August 31, 1931, there had been 327,990 men employed doing 7,228.744 so-called man-days' work. According to the statement made by the Minister of Labour the other day from August 31, 1931, up to January 31,	1932, there were
334,301 men employed for 7,415,973 man-days. That means that for that first period every man worked an average of 22 1/20 days -dividing the number of men into the number of man-days; and for the latter period, up to January 31, 1932, there were provided 22} days for each man, or a little over 44 days' work per man during the combined periods. Therefore as a result of this unemployment relief measure, during the period from October 1, 1930, to January 31, 1931, roughly four hundred working days, there has been supplied only three days' work out of a month to the men who have been given employment. Am I not correct in saying that the act has proved
to be pitiably inadequate to provide employment for the great number of men who are out of work? I think any measure which could not provide more than three days' work a month for the number of men who apparently are idle is a measure which has not succeeded to a very great degree in satisfying the undertakings which were made by the Prime Minister at the time of the election.
That is the result as far as the provision of employment is concerned. It means that work was provided for ten per cent of the time for six per cent of the population of Canada by this measure which was to provide work for all who were willing to work-work and not doles-and which was to end unemployment. Now let us look at the cost, and here is where I find some difficulty, because my right hon. friend the Prime Minister says it is not all expended as yet. However, taking the amounts as given by the Minister of Labour the other day, I find that there was spent or committed for some $146,899,219 by federal, provincial and municipal governments.

No; my friend the Minister of Labour was the one who gave the figures, and I did not hear him say anything about railways. As I say, there was spent some $146,899,219. To employ all those men at 83 per day for the 14,000,000 odd man-days- that is, combining the two groups of man-days of about 7,000,000 each, you would have spent something like $44,000,000 instead of $146,000,000. Someone may say the difference is made up by the cost of materials. It is a pretty large percentage for materials-that is, if you assume that $100,000,000 out of the $146,000,000 was spent on materials. Possibly it may not have been spent, as my right hon. friend says; we only have the statement made by the Minister of Labour, but this fact remains, that to pay those men $3 a day for every day they worked would have cost $44,000,000; and the next fact is that according to the Minister of Labour we have committed ourselves to spend, or have spent, some $146,000,000, or three times the amount spent for labour. Possibly much of that went for materials, but does anyone say that those who produced the materials are necessarily those for whom employment should be provided? This money was a special vote for the purpose of providing employment for

Unemployment Continuance Act
those specially in need, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it has got a long way beyond that when we have spent $100,000,000 more than would actually be necessary to pay the men for every day worked under this scheme.
Now, with regard to the effect, the other day my right hon. leader quoted figures to show that there is a decreasing line of index figures of employment in practically every vocation; that we are without rejuvenation of industry, notwithstanding the tariff; that we are far from being back to the days of 1927 or 1928, or even 1926 as far as employment is concerned. I could give, Mr. Speaker, many figures which are published in the statement of the Bureau of Statistics, but I will content myself with placing on Hansard just one series of figures which appear in the February statement, just issued. I refer to the index numbers of employment by economic areas, and I will give the figures for five dates, January 1, 1930, January 1, 1931, February 1,
1931,	January 1, 1932, and February 1, 1932. For the whole of Canada the employment figure on January 1, 1930, was 111-2; on January 1, 1931, it had gone down 10 points, and was 101-7; on February 1, 1931, it had gone down another point and was 100-7; on January 1, 1932, it was 91-6, and on February 1,
1932,	it was 89-7, which does not show much success in providing employment as far as industry is concerned. Someone may ask what figures I can give with regard to employment generally, with regard to the labouring classes. I have inquired, but I am unable to find any survey made by this government since last September which would give us any idea of how many unemployed there are in this country at this time. There was an estimate made of something like 330,000, I think, in September last, but from that time on we have had no information whatever and no one can tell. But I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if anyone needs to have statistics quoted to show that there is unemployment in this country at the present time. All you have to do is ask the federated charities; ask the Red Cross; ask the relief societies; ask the citizens' committees; go out on the street, and you will know whether unemployment has been lessened or whether it has been even improved as a result of the legislation we are asked to renew.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the scheme has failed as far as providing work for any great number of men over any sustained period is concerned; it has failed as far as cost is concerned; it has failed because the figures of employment have gone down instead of increasing; it has failed to show any improve-
ment in the unemployment situation, and lastly the scheme has failed also in that in a great many cases it has not reached the people for whom it was intended. To-night I do not propose to go into a number of individual cases, but I want to make a statement with regard to some cases which have come to my notice and which have been brought to my attention, in order to indicate at least in some instances what has happened with regard to this money. Cases have been brought to my attention in which men with bank accounts were given employment; men in good circumstances have been given work in connection with unemployment relief. One case brought to my attention was that of a man so well off that he was able to loan money to the school section. Work has been given single men with no responsibilities whatever. Men of this kind have been taken on in connection with unemployment relief work in the section of the country which I happen to represent, and they have kept out of work sons of widowed mothers who were the only support of the family; returned soldiers in need; men with large families of from five to nine children who had to get help from their neighbours. These have not been allowed to work, while men of the class to which I have referred have been taken on these jobs supposed to have been provided for those most in need.
I am not suggesting that this has been universal; I certainly hope it has not, but I am saying that it has resulted from the lack of supervision which I brought to the attention of the former Minister of Labour myself. I came to Ottawa to see his officers in an endeavour to have these things run in such a way that those who needed work should have it, but I am sorry to say that at least in a number of instances that idea has not been carried out. I think the right hon. Prime Minister perhaps has not grasped the situation when he speaks in generalities and says that by and large the thing has been well done. The individual we have been trying to reach is the man hard up, the man down and out, the man who is destitute, the man whose family is in need. It does not do him any good to say that a large part of the money has been well spent, or something like that. The thing is that he has been left off the job; his family are in want and have to be helped by neighbours, while others in good circumstances are taken on.
That situation could be cured only in one wayr. It could not be cured with people staying here in Ottawa and issuing orders. It could not be cured by passing orders in council; one such order in council was passed.

The only way to cure it is to evolve a system whereby the work in the community will be dealt out and apportioned by some independent body like the Red Cross, the overseers of the poor, a citizens' committee or something of the kind which knows conditions in that locality and is able to say, "This man is in a more needy position than the other man and we do not care anything about the man's race, colour, politics or religion. Unfortunately that has not been done; all the orders in council that were issued from Ottawa, and all the supervision that was attempted to be carried on from here did not help one little bit to get that man who needed work a position, so long as the actual dealing out of the work, the apportioning of the work, was left to the local patronage committee in the particular neighbourhood where the work was going on.
Now that is what has taken place; that is the complaint I have with regard to even the number of men mentioned here who are supposed to have got work. There were a good many of them who were in a very much better position financially than many of their neighbours who were refused work because of political partisanship on the part of those who actually had charge or took charge of selecting those who were to be taken on. And it could not be otherwise so long as you had, in a great many cases, men who needed work kept standing outside a Conservative government committee room, waiting to hear whether or not their names were going to be put on the pay-roll in connection with the job. So long as that was the situation you could not have a fair distribution of the work. In many cases this was not done, but in many cases it was done; and I say, regardless of the fact that hon. gentlemen who occupy the government benches may have had the best intentions, the result has been that in many instances the work has failed to go to those for whom it was intended.
I brought to the notice of the Minister of Labour some of these very matters and asked him to investigate it; I asked him whether he would not appoint someone altogether outside the realm of political patronage. In connection with an ordinary public work, if the friends of those in power happen to be put on the job, very well; I am not making any complaint. But when money is voted for people who are unemployed and destitute, and an order in council is passed providing that the money shall be given to those who need it, the government cannot go too far in seeing to it that that intention and that
spirit is carried out and that those should be given jobs who are in need of work.
What is suggested to be done here is that this act which has not worked out in practice, shall be resuscitated, resurrected and once more put into force. My right hon. leader has shown more clearly than I can why this piece of legislation should be rejected at this time and why the suggestion which he has made should be accepted with regard to assisting those in want. Last year we protested and warned our friends that this was not the sort of legislation to pass in the year 1932. We pointed out that there was no need of taking the powers contained in this act. Well I remember the night the Solicitor General, a member of this government, dared us to vote against the bill. He intimated that if we voted against it it would be said that we were taking the bread out of the mouths of women and children, and he dared us to oppose the bill. We did not vote against the bill but we protested as strongly as we could and told him that notwithstanding the fact that it was against our ideas of responsible government we would vote for it in order to see that the object at which it aimed would be accomplished. That evidently has been taken as a sign of weakness. As my right hon. leader suggested this afternoon, the government should not ask us to do it again. An offer has been made whereby money will be provided without stint to take care of the present situation, and I submit that the Prime Minister and his government should seriously consider that offer. What is the situation? It is proposed now that we shall pass an act vesting all the powers of the federal parliament, as to peace, order and good government in Canada, in hon. gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches, and that, forsooth, while we are sitting in this House of Commons, sent here supposedly by the people to represent them under the constitutional prerogative which is theirs, while we are actually sitting here our friends on the treasury benches may be over in the east block passing an order in council to send an expeditionary force to China under the provisions of that act. While we were actually assembled that might be done. An hon. member suggests that this is preposterous. It may be preposterous; nevertheless that is the exact position. And what is more-

Suppose they make a treaty; well, it has already been done, and they are merely locking the stable after the horse is stolen. My right hon. friend knows that in England they have passed the Abnormal Imports Bill, giving the government power to make certain regulations with regard to certain imports; and they have been so careful about it that the government is required to lay the order in council on the table of the house and if it is not ratified within twenty-eight days it ceases to be law. The Prime Minister does not even offer us that sop in connection with this legislation. He proposes to be able to pass orders in council and will merely lay it on the table and tell us it has been done. That is not constitutional government, and there is nothing at this time that requires the passage of any such legislation.
A good deal has been said about the blank cheque. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I only want to refer to a rule with which you are

more familiar than the rest of us. We are asked to pass a bill giving to our friends unlimited power to vote unlimited amounts of money. Here is the rule which governs us in matters of this sort-standing order 61:
All aids and supplies granted to His Majesty by the parliament of Canada, are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the house, as it is the undoubted right of the bouse to direct, limit, and appoint m all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
That is the power we want to exercise, to direct and limit, to prescribe limitations and qualifications of the grant. But my hon. friends opposite propose that we shall give up that right entirely and hand it over to them, even though we may happen to be in session at the time.
The Prime Minister regaled us this afternoon with a few decisions of the privy council with respect to constitutional matters. I am not going to deal with them now, but with all due deference to him I do not think they had a great deal to do with the discussion in connection with this bill. They did indicate that the War Measures Act had been held to be intra vires of this parliament. No one is suggesting that this act is not intra vires in the wide terms in which it is framed. My right hon. friend read a passage to the effect that the government had some discretion in deciding whether the time of emergency had actually come. But let me read to him a decision with regard to the rights of the House of Commons and the limitations upon the executive with respect both to the taxation of the people and the expenditure of the people's money. This was a case that occurred in England during the war, and it came under the Defence of the Realm Act. A regulation had been made whereby the food controller could regulate the sale and distribution of *milk. The food controller had imposed upon one particular individual a tax of two pence per gallon in connection with the distribution of milk in a certain area, and the individual had agreed to pay. Upon being advised afterwards that it was unconstitutional and ultra vires the individual refused to live up to his agreement and the result, in short, was that the crown failed to recover. Why? Because if an act does not in the most express terms give away to the executive the powers of parliament, those powers shall be held not to have been surrendered. The following is a passage from the judgment of Lord Atkin:
No power to make a charge upon the subject for the use of the crown could arise except by

We know how strictly parliament has maintained this right- and, in particular, how jealously the House of Commons has asserted its predominance in the power of raising money. An elaborate custom of parliament has prevailed by which money for the service of the crown is only granted at the request of the crown made by a responsible minister and assented to by a resolution of the house in committee. By constitutional usage no money proposal can be altered by the second chamber, whose powers are confined to acceptance or rejection.

Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part to-night in this debate may I say that I do not think there has been a question before this house for years which included in its make-up so many angles which any Liberal would like to discuss. In discussing this question of the administration during the past year of unemployment and farm relief, may I touch upon a point or two raised this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). He made the statement that there must be a clear line of demarcation between dominion and provincial jurisdiction, and went on to argue that apart from the promises made in 1930 the policy of the government since coming into office has been to deal with this unemployment problem and this relief question largely in a municipal and provincial manner. It is true the federal government has taken action but that action has been anything but purely national action and, therefore, the promises and pledges given to the people in the elections have not been adhered to. I am at a loss to know just where the Prime Minister stands on the question of jurisdiction, provincially or nationally, because he has made more than one pronouncement in this house which has left considerable doubt. Sometimes he stands for the supremacy of the provinces, sometimes he stands for the supremacy of the dominion, and at other times he throws the one-into the other and tells us that the both combined can do practically anything as far as the public funds of -the -country are concerned.
Apart from the constitutional question, there is a moral obligation devolving upon the Prime Minister and his government, but that fact was by no means emphasized this afternoon strongly enough. The Prime Minister dealt with the taking of notes from those granted relief; he argued that these notes were taken so that the relief need not be considered as charity. The danger is that these notes will constitute a political hold upon the individual during elections, and this is a danger to democracy and to the wise expenditure of public funds. I am opposed to that principle and I do not believe the government will gain one cent by the taking of these notes from the destitute farmers in western Canada.

These men, once they understand the situation, will do their best to repay the government if they ever should have money, and I believe that they would pay the government more willingly without a note than they will with one. Much of this money will never be repaid, so why have notes signed? That is a question which will have to be explained so that destitute western farmers from whom these notes have been peremptorily demanded will know exactly the reason why they have had to give them.
This afternoon the Prime Minister admitted that in asking for approval of this resolution upon which a bill will be 'based he was asking for authority outside of the ordinary authority constituted in any Canadian parliament. That is an important admission. It is so important that it brings before us the whole development of responsible government in this country. I am one of those who say that apart from the development of constitutional government in this dominion, there is not much else nationally worth while. If we throw to the winds the results of the fight our forefathers made to win the rights of responsible and representative government in Canada, we have not much left. In 1840, when we were handed a constitution, and when the right of responsible government was won in this country, we thought we had passed forever any days like those through which we are now passing; we thought the question of responsible government was settled for good, although in 1843 it was taken away and then restored in 1849. But from 1849 on we did not think the head of any government, Liberal or Conservative, or whatever the party-in power might be, would ever, at least in our national legislature, dare infringe upon parliamentary usages and powers as was done last year and as is being done now.
Therefore I say that it devolves upon us on this side of the house to oppose any move for any authority that we do not think is necessary, any move to take away from parliament any sovereign authority it possesses, any move to take away from the members who are here their rights under the constitution, because those rights have been guaranteed and have been handed down to us from generation to generation. Consequently, although we on this side of the house are prepared to vote without any delay or procrastination, any amount of money that is absolutely required for seed and feed, yet, if the Prime Minister of the day will not so arrange his legislation that the idea of giving the executive too much authority is eliminated, nothing is left for us to do but to oppose such unwarranted autocracy and to oppose it to the bitter end.

In speaking on the question of unemployment, I think it might be well to get a historic perspective of unemployment conditions in Canada during the last few decades. Prior to 1896, after the Conservatives had been in power, almost eighteen years from 1878, what were the conditions in this country? We know commerce was at a low ebb; we know that industry was practically strangled; we know that deficit after deficit was shown by the government of the day every time the house would meet, and we know that the great west was not even opened up under the high tariff of the past. We know Canada was discouraged and by 1896 the 'business of the country was almost at a standstill. Then the people of Canada took it into their hands to deal with the question of unemployment, to deal with a tariff machine the working of which had baffled the Conservatives, and questions that the powers of the day could not successfully face themselves. At that time the people of Canada defeated the government that was then in power and put a Liberal government in its place. What was the result? For the next number of years unemployment disappeared; there was no unemployment from 1896 to 1911. There was progress all along the line, industrially and commercially, and Canada developed and progressed as never before.
Then in 1913, under a Conservative government again, we find unemployment coming to the fore. We find another depression which lapsed when the great war began. But in 1920 and 1921, after Conservative rule for ten years, unemployment conditions again developed in Canada, and before the people could acquire control of the situation we had deficits as in days gone by. In 1920 there was a deficit of 892,000,000; in 1921 there was a deficit of $81,000,000, so that you have in two years a deficit of almost $200,000,000. Along with these deficits there was unemployment. Commerce was at a standstill as previously; industry was not developing, and consequently the country was not progressing nor was it as prosperous as it should be. Again the people of Canada took things into their hands, and in the election of 1921 the government of the day was defeated and the Liberals were returned to power.
The Liberals remained in power from 1921 until 1930. What were the conditions during those nine years? It did not take long for deficits to disappear. From 1924 on there were no more deficits. Trade grew as it had never grown before. There was prosperity abroad in the land. Unemployment disappeared and was an unknown quantity for nine years. The reason was that there was

in power a party that had a Liberal policy, a policy that tapped the resources of the world and linked Canada up with them, that tapped the resources of the empire and linked Canada up with them, a policy that encouraged trade within the confines of the dominion.
It might be well to point out that prior to 1930, even though times were prosperous and conditions were good, a very important world situation was developing and that world situation, so far as strangling trade is concerned, was caused by the erection of tariff walls practically all around the world. The erection of those tariff walls produced such a situation in the markets of the world that every nation was out for himself, out for the principle of economic nationalism, out for the principle of self-sufficiency, which in the last analysis always proves wrong. In this case it proved wrong too, helping to develop an international situation that was dangerous. What did our opponents say? They said:	Here
we have a party in power and a situation developing and we are going to hold them responsible for the whole thing. In 1928 and 1929 they went across Canada from ocean to ocean, and what did they say? They blamed the condition that was developing upon the Liberal prime minister of the day, upon the Liberal party, upon the policy of the Liberal party. They said:	Unless you remove this
party from power; unless you have a change of policy; unless you have Conservative high tariffs rather than Liberal trade treaties and Liberal low tariffs, you are going to have national destruction follow in the train of the party in power-follow in the wake of Liberalism. So they went from one part of Canada to the other, and by their talk and exhortation and declamations they practically undermined trade, commerce and industry in the dominion, with the result that by the time the election took place in 1930 a situation had developed that was somewhat dangerous. What did they assert? They asserted: This is not a world situation; this is a national condition, and it has been brought about by the policies of the Liberal party, by the Liberal party as a governing force in Canada, and therefore that party ought to be defeated. They went out in the election; they carried that fight into the election, and there is no question that they made a political football of unemployment.
In May, 1930, the unemployment index in Canada was practically 9 per cent, whereas in the United States it was 20 per cent, and in Great Britain 14 per cent. For the next two or three months that unemployment index remained practically stationary. After the 41761

Never before in the history of Canada did it grow with such rapidity. The result was that conditions became worse and worse until the time of the special session of parliament when there were 200,000 unemployed.
What policy do we find hon. gentlemen opposite evolving to meet the unemployment situation? We know they did only one thing, they had only one policy, a policy sixty years old, the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald involving high tariffs, restricted markets, exploitation of individuals, and so on. They said, "If this cannot cure unemployment, nothing will." So they went to work and raised the tariff wall sky high around Canada, they did exactly what the other nations of the world had been foolishly doing; they played the high tariff game to the limit and it is no wonder to-night that we find they have sown to the wind and reaped the whirlwind. Last year they deliberately raised the tariff, schedule after schedule, where lower tariffs had1 been in effect for years.

The subject was further dealt with in 1930, when the committee brought in a report which after a spirited debate was endorsed by the house. The committee stated that it was no use to inaugurate a system of unemployment insurance unless a number of the provinces cooperated. The committee stated further that they felt the need of statistical data on unemployment and employment and recommended that at the next census provision should be made to secure such data.
When that report was before the house the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Liberal party endorsed it, but only after a long debate on an amendment that was defeated did the opposition allow the main motion to be accepted on division. That meant they were opposed to the report-to

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take exception in the strongest possible manner to the resolution now before the house. I do so for several reasons, the first of which is that it leaves entirely unsettled and undetermined the principle of the unemployment and farm relief policy of the government of Canada. This government has been in power since the middle of 1930. They started out with a more or less well defined policy for the relief of unemployment through the construction of public works, but of course that policy was not new. I can remember hearing it advocated in this house during the last parliament, when the country was enjoying a very considerable measure of prosperity. There were a few members who said that in days of great surpluses we should not construct public works on an extensive scale but should lay up our money against the day when we would have adversity, and then we could spend it for the relief of the unemployed for whom we might have to provide.
When the government came into power they adopted that as their policy; at the emergency session of 1930 we were asked to vote and did vote $20,000,000 for the relief of unemployment. From that time until the end of the fiscal year on March 31, 1931, something more than $17,000,000 was either expended or appropriated for the relief of unemployment, and almost that entire sum was devoted to the construction of public works. The policy of constructing public works in order to relieve unemployment has certain apparent advantages. In the first place it gives wages to the unemployed and provides purchasing power which otherwise they would not have; in the second place it provides a market for materials, and in the third place it gives a stimulus to business in the localities where the works are carried on. At present in the United States of America there are many prominent public men who advocate the adoption of a similar policy, but the federal government of that country has not seen fit to do so on any large scale.
During the last few months there has been a considerable amount of discussion in the
papers and before the public as to the advisability of continuing the policy of spending money on public works for the relief of unemployment. It is urged 'that this is a most expensive policy; it has been pointed out that since	last	August	for	every man-dayof work that has been supplied the unemployed of	this	country, something like $10has been spent by our various governments. If we consider the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) we find that it works out to about this figure. Speaking in the house during a debate a few days ago the minister gave the total amount spent from August 1,	1931,	to the	end	of February ofthis year,	and he also gave	the number of
man-days of work during that time. The result of those two figures, as I have indicated, shows that not this government alone but all governments in Canada, federal, provincial and municipal, have paid about $10 for every man-day of work that has been supplied.
The financial papers particularly have taken exception to that policy. A fair example of the criticism one finds in those newspapers is found in the Financial Post of November 14, 1931, under the heading The Nation's Business. This is what the Post says:
There is an idea that all this huge expenditure of government funds is creating prosperity. It is doing nothing of the sort; it is creating a worse crisis than the one it is designed to relieve. One may question that the expenditure of public money is even adding to the total of jobs that are available. We are given extensive figures to show how many men have been put to work on relief programs. But we will never know how many of these men are being denied the privilege of working at their regular jobs or on new private projects because the threat of high taxation and the freezing up of bond markets is holding back normal business development. Many institutions in Canada have large buildings planned and will go ahead with them as soon as they can see light; but they will not be able to see light so long as our governments endanger the credit basis of the country by their unchecked spending schemes. It may indeed be that every government job created now causes a private job to disappear.
Hence agitation has arisen, more or less extensive, for an alteration in the policy of the government. A policy is now being urged upon the government of confining our assistance to direct relief alone, a policy of curtailment of public expenditures, thrift, economy, reduction of the civil service, reduction in the salaries of the civil service and a decrease in expenditures on public works to the irreducible minimum. My criticism of the government, and it seems to me that it is an unanswerable criticism, is that the government, from the very time it assumed office, has never pursued

It seems to be in a muddle and has no cleareut conception of what the policy of this country should be, whether it should be a policy of expenditures or a policy of retrenchment. I suggest, therefore, that before the Prime Minister comes before this house, as he does to-day, and asks for a renewal of the dictatorship mandate, so-called, he should lay before the house the fundamental principle-I do not mean the details-upon which he proposes to proceed during the coming months.
I said that the government has not been consistent. Let me illustrate what I mean by that. We appropriated something over $17,000,000 between the emergency session of 1930 and the end of the fiscal year March 31, 1931; but when the public works estimates were brought down in the following spring we found that in the estimates for 1932 there was a decrease in the appropriations for public works as compared with the preceding year of $17,694,166.31. That is to say, while with the one hand the government was spending about $17,000,000 on the expenditure theory for the relief of unemployment and the relief of depression, it was curtailing expenditures in the Public Works department alone to the extent of a little over $17,000,000 on the thrift, eoonomy and retrenchment theory. In other words, what the Department of Public Works was doing the Department of Labour was undoing; or, if you like to put it the other way, what the Department of Labour was doing the Department of Public Works was undoing. There has been no consistency in the government's policy.
The Prime Minister reaffirmed the expenditure policy at the end of the session of 1931. At the end of July or August 1, 1931. he came before the house and, in asking for the very bill which we are asked to extend today, he said that the government would continue its policy of constructing public works for the relief of unemployment. And he told us in this debate this afternoon that a great many expenditures on public works had been made in various parts of Canada. Moreover, when the Public Works estimates were up not long ago the Minister of Public Works justified certain isolated projects in various constituencies of the dominion on the ground that they were necessary for the relief of unemployment. I do not want to go into that particularly, but one that will occur to us is the Haileybury breakwater expenditure of $45,000 which was justified on the ground that it was necessary for the relief of unemployment. But at the same time, in the public works estimates for the year 1933,

we find a reduction in public works appropriations as compared with the previous year of $10,120,000 odd. So that we see that the policy of the government has not only been inconsistent from the time hon. gentlemen opposite took office, but it has not been uniform in various parts of Canada. It varies from place to place and from time to time and at the same time. It is impossible for the government to make any progress if they concurrently pursue two entirely incompatible, inconsistent and contrary policies. Moreover, before the Prime Minister asks the house to give him another blank cheque and to give to his government power to legislate for the Dominion of Canada, he should say by what principle he is going to be guided. What is the principle that is to guide him with reference to these expenditures in the future?
I have another objection to the resolution, and that is that it does not take into account certain emergent situations which are arising in various parts of Canada. We know that there is an emergent situation in the west; there has been since the very serious weather conditions of the year 1931; and the government has taken hold of that situation and has been careful to meet it to the best of its ability. But situations are arising elsewhere which should be brought before the House of Commons-not before the members of the government, the cabinet council, but before this House of Commons. Very little has been said by members from the maritime provinces about conditions in that part of the country. I gather the impression, from persons with whom I have talked, that they think that the maritime provinces are in a comparatively prosperous condition. I was pleased to hear to-day that Quebec and the maritime provinces did not require any direct assistance to their governments from the federal government, while this fact was not true of any other province in Canada. But let me say to the Prime Minister, to the government and to this house-

I submit that the most serious objection to be taken to this resolution is that a violation of the constitutional rights of the members of this house is being sought by the government of the day. It is hard to find words strong enough to characterize the action of the government in attempting to put through this resolution. It was bad enough in the emergency session of 1930 to ask for a vote of $20,000,000 for works which were not specified; it was worse in the session of 1931 to get from this parliament a blank cheque and legislation which set up a dictatorship between sessions, but it is infinitely worse for the government to have the temerity to come before this house and seek to perpetuate that dictatorship while parliament is in session,
This matter was up for discussion during the latter part of July and the first part of August, 1931. At that time we objected to certain features of certain sections of the act. The first objectionable feature with which we dealt was that no limitation was placed upon the powers of the government. Section 4 of the act reads as follows:
The governor in council shall have full power to make all such orders and regulations as may be deemed necessary or desirable for relieving distress, providing employment and, within the competence of parliament, maintaining peace, order and good government throughout Canada.
In other words, the government was granted all the powers of parliament itself. It means that a bill passed by this house and the other chamber and assented to by His Excellency may be repealed the next day by the government sitting over in the east block or wheT-ever it functions. They are permitted to go fair in the face of the wishes of this House of Commons; they can pass an order in council repealing legislation which the house has adapted. There has never been anything so outrageous in the history of this country. It may be said that they would not do that, but we can point to many instances where something almost as bad has been done between sessions, and to this I will refer a little later.
The second objectionable feature in the act was that there was no limitation either of the amount which could be expended or of the purpose for which it should be used. Section 2 reads as follows:
There may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund such moneys as the governor in council in his discretion may deem expedient to expend for relieving distress, providing employment and maintaining within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada.

The third objectionable feature was that power was being granted to create new crimes, to set up extraordinary courts and to prescribe new and unusual modes of procedure. Section 5 reads:
All orders and regulations of the governor in council shall have the force of law and shall be enforced in such manner and by such court officers and authorities as the governor in council may prescribe, and may be varied, extended or revoked by any subsequent order or regulation;
That is, the right of trial by jury might be taken away, or might be granted where it was not applicable. The section continues:
-but if any order or regulation is varied, extended or revoked, neither the previous operation thereof nor anything duly done thereunder shall be affected thereby, nor shall any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred thereunder be affected by any such variation, extension or revocation.
The fourth feature in the act to which we objected was that by implication it granted power to repeal existing legislation. Section 3 reads:
Without restricting the generality of the terms of the next preceding section hereof, and notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law, the governor in council may,-
The section goes on to outline the powers granted notwithstanding the provisions of any other statute. It is clear that under this section the government has power to repeal by order in council the legislation of this parliament.
These were the main objectionable features which were pointed out when the act was passed. If there was any justification for such sweeping legislation it was because of the nearness of prorogation, but certainly there is no justification to-day, when we are practically beginning a new session, for the extension of that legislation. At that time we said that the act attempted to take away from parliament matters which should be under its exclusive control, that it established a virtual dictatorship, that it violated the basic principles of the control of parliament over national expenditure, that it was more sweeping than the war measures of the government of Sir Robert Borden, that it was a piece of despotism without parallel in the history of Canada, and that it was the worst piece of autocratic power which a Prime Minister or government of this country had ever attempted1 to assume. All that was true, and it is doubly true to-day when similar legislation is being sought while we, the duly constituted and elected representatives of th* people, are

I do not know upon what grounds this legislation can be justified. I understood from the Prime Minister yesterday that to-day he would give us some reasons why he would prefer to take this course rather than to proceed in the regular way by means of a supply bill. I listened to his address this afternoon but the reasons were not forthcoming. He said nothing in his speech to indicate where the advantage would be in proceeding by this method rather than by a supply bill. The only measures which he forecast were measures of expenditure, the only amount which he mentioned was one not exceeding six or seven millions of dollars. If the right hon. gentleman desires merely to spend a few million dollars, why does he not name a sum abundantly sufficient to cover his requirements? If he did, we in opposition would be willing to vote that amount. What reason is there for taking to himself and his colleagues the power to legislate? What reason is there for taking from us the power to do that which by constitution we are elected to do? None whatever has been suggested. Why should the government have power to amend and repeal this and the other act and then come to parliament and say: it is a fait accompli; there is the order in council; the thing is done and you can like it or lump it; criticize if you will, but it is all over. No reason was given by the Prime Minister this afternoon and I suggest no reason can be given. Last summer certain reasons were advanced. First, he said that between sessions he did not know how much money he would require. The answer made to him then is the answer we give him to-day: Make the sum large enough and we will vote it. To that very reasonable proposal he turns a deaf ear; for reasons that have not been given, he rejects it.
Last summer another reason advanced for the passage of this legislation was that all sorts of things might happen before the next session. The Prime Minister did not know exactly what might happen. He thought there might be some agitation in the country; he hinted at some disaffection among the labouring people, and that it might be necessary to take these extraordinary powers in order to deal with that situation.

I challenge him to produce it.
