I am not addressing myself to the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Price); when I do it will be time enough for him to reply. I challenge the Minister of

Labour to produce details of the expenditure of the $47,000 granted the county of Gloucester under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, and if he does I will show him where and how the work was done. I reiterate, the work I am going to refer to was done under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, and there can be no doubt about it. The other night I gave the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) credit for the way in which he acted in the matter. He put a stop to irregularities, but the Minister of Labour never undertook to do anything. The work on the Grande Anse breakwater was unemployment relief work done under the direction of the federal department of Public Works. Why did I complain there? This is one of the reasons. I found that on that work the foreman named Theriault had his two sons employed.
What of that?
Order.

That was in direct violation of the orders issued by the Department of Public Works. When it was reported to the minister of that department he looked mto it and had the irregularity stopped. We have another case of a father and his son sixteen years of age at work, while another man with a family of seven children was denied work.

Will the hon. gentleman
allow a question?

No, I will not. That man
was turned down and told distinctly that he was on the wrong political side. The resident engineer in St. John was instructed to look into the matter. He did, and the foreman had to admit that he had used that language. We have numerous similar cases in connection with works carried on in the county of Gloucester.
The other night I said that the government had not displayed sufficient care in approving of the relief project. Let me emphasize that to-night. I hold in my hand a return laid on the table embracing all the projects accepted by the federal government for work for unemployment relief in the county of Gloucester. I have before me a statement of projects accepted by the Department of Labour covering an expenditure of $750,000 for unemployment relief work in New Brunswick. The date of approval is November 26, 1931. Three quarters of the money was spent months before the federal

Unemployment Continuance Act
government ever approved of the projects. I have here particulars of $26,500 to be spent in the county of Gloucester, and approved on November 26, 1931. Every oent of that money was spent before that date.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Was it well spent?

No, it was not. That is
what I am complaining about, and if the minister will give me a proper investigation, if he will name a commissioner to come to Gloucester county with a detailed statement of the money spent there under unemployment relief, I will undertake to prove under oath the statements I am making to-night. What more do we find? They lacked sufficient care in approving of these projects. In the list of projects approved on November 26, 1931, we find the town of Sunny Brae, with the amount of $1,750. That money was all spent before the Department of Labour approved of that project.

The hon. gentleman would
not dare make that statement in the city of Moncton.

Yes, I will make it in
Sunny Brae. Take the money spent in Gloucester, Northumberland, Restigouche and many of the other counties; you will find that it was expended before approval was given.
You would not dare say that in New Brunswick.
I would say it anywhere.
No, you would not dare.

Mr. Speaker, surely I am
entitled to speak for forty minutes without interruption by the hon. member for Westmorland. I am sorry he thinks it is his duty to interrupt me; I would rather see him stand up and defend his constituents and plead for their rights, especially the rights of the railway men who elected him.
I will do it, and I will take you to task for attacking Barachois and Aboujagan.

I never attacked them; I
asked for information. Surely as a member of this house I am entitled to that information, and when it comes down my hon. friend may not be so proud of it.
Now, sir, let me point out another injustice that has been done in Gloucester county. The incorporated town of Bathurst, with a population of about five thousand, undertook to pave all the streets in order to relieve unemployment, at an expenditure of $225,000.
When this work was almost completed they applied for a share of the federal money under this act, but their request was refused. Work remained to be done to the extent of about $28,000, and when the town applied for assistance in completing that work their request was approved and they received $7,500. While Bathurst was doing work to the extent of $225,000, in order to relieve unemployment, with not a dollar contributed by the federal government, other towns which had completed the work planned before November 26 were paid the full federal share of the cost of those works. So to my mind this act has not been administered in an honest and fair way.
This afternoon the right hon. Prime Minister stated that at a certain public meeting in the county of Gloucester I told the people that I had received letters from the federal Department of Labour asking for recommendations as to the work which should be undertaken in Gloucester county in order to relieve unemployment, and that I flaunted those letters before my audience and said I was the one who should look after that. I then interjected that the Prime Minister had been misinformed. I think that information was given to the right hon. gentleman within the last forty-eight or seventy-two hours, and I wish to tell him that whoever made those statements to him led him astray, because there is not one word of truth in them. It is true that I did read in public the letters sent me by the Department of Labour; I did read in public the regulations under which this money was to be spent, and I explained to the people that there was to be no discrimination, political, racial or religious. There was a by-election going on, and I explained that everyone working on the roads had a perfect right to vote as he saw fit, that this money was not the money of Liberals or Conservatives; it was money voted by the parliament of Canada to help the unemployed in that county. What happened when I was making that explanation? The letter from which I am reading now is on file in the Department of Labour, and it contains this statement will regard to the parish of Beresford:
That all the supervisors of roads in this parish were acting in the same way as did Supervisor Cormier, I may say that on October 18th I was addressing a public meeting in the parish hall at Petit Roeher on behalf of the opposition candidate. I had been asked a question touching the expenditure of unemployment relief money. I was explaining that the instructions issued by the federal Department of Labour set forth very plainly that there was to be no discrimination whatever along political lines in the expenditure of this money, that

Unemployment Continuance Act
this money should be earned by those really in need of it, and that no matter what might be said by the other side, everyone was free to vote as he saw fit notwithstanding that he might be employed under the supervision of the provincial government. I was flatly contradicted by a man in the audience, and when I inquired who the person was he did not hesitate to come forward and inform me that he was a supervisor of roads and would have charge of this expenditure, and added "Pas un seul Liberal aura de 1'ouvrage de chomage. C'est Coffyn, et non pas Yeniot qui verra a cela." And this supervisor certainly did keep his word.
He said, "Not a single Liberal will have any part of this unemployment work. It is Doctor Coffyn"-who was the provincial government candidate-"that will look after it and not P. J. Veniot."
That partisanship was carried on throughout the length and breadth of the county of Gloucester. There was a by-election in that county; the Premier of New Brunswick addressed a public meeting in the town of Bathurst on the Friday night before the election, and said:
We do not want Doctor Coffyn elected in Gloucester because we need his vote to maintain the government in power. We want him elected so that we will have reason to do something big for Gloucester county along the lines of the unemployment relief aid to be given by the federal government and the province of New Brunswick.
There was a bribe held out to the electors of that county; they were told that unless Doctor Coffyn was elected, unless they returned a man who was favourable to the government, the government would measure the relief to be doled out in Gloucester county by the actions of the electors on polling day.

I don't believe the premier
ever made such a statement.

And I know you would
say, if he did make it, that he had no right to make it, wouldn't you?
I would simply say just now that he didn't make it.
He did make it. The hon. gentleman has no right under the rules of the house to question my veracity.
He didn't make such a statement.

Let me go a step further.
I hold in my hand a letter over the signature of W. H. Coffyn, provincial candidate in the

county. This is addressed to Supervisor Max Arseneau. Here is the letter:
Six Roads, October 24, 1931. Supervisor Max Arseneau:
Please see that Peter Gauvin has work on the road when you do your work next. It will be to our mutual advantage.
(Signed) W. H. Coffyn.
Is that another provincial employee?

They are all provincial
employees who spent the unemployment relief money in New Brunswick. That is the reason I object to it; that is why I say politics is creeping into the expenditure of the money, and it should not be allowed. But I go further than that. Just to show the opinion that is spreading among the people, that this unemployment relief money is to be expended along political lines, I have an extract from a letter which I am going to read:
I was successful in getting the amount authorized for expenditure in your district, but the patronage is entirely in the hands of the four defeated candidates.
I would advise you to take up the matter direct with them, as I regret that I have nothing whatever to do with provincial matters, and this work is being done entirely through them, although the federal is contributing; unfortunately I have no say whatever as to patronage in the local.
By whom is that signed?

Without being saucy to
the hon. gentleman I may tell him it is none of his business. Now there is an example of how patronage came into the distribution of this unemployment relief money. That is signed by a federal member. Here is a man who is writing for work; he writes to get an order to go to work. He cannot get it without an order and he is told, "If you want an order you will have to go to the four provincial candidates defeated in the provincial election." Do you mean to tell me that under conditions of that kind, I can approve of or support the same system that was in practice last year and which evidently is to be put into practice this year? The unemployment relief money was used as a political fund in Gloucester county.
There was another by-election in the province of New Brunswick, in the county of St. John. There are only about eleven or twelve thousand inhabitants, and for the money that is on this list as having been approved of on November 26, 1931, and in 1930 work was done in the county of St. John to the extent of $52,000.

Unemployment Relief
When was that by-election?
Last year.
Before the money was voted by this parliament?
Yes, quite true.
There was not a cent spent in the county of St. John.
Don't be too quick. I have here proof that work in the county of St. John was done to the extent of practically $52,000.

But long
after the by-election.

That was approved November 26, and every cent of the money was spent during the summer time and a lot of it during the election; and that money spent in the county of St. John during that by-election was transferred to the projects submitted to the federal government and approved November 26, 1931. I am sorry to say that the hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about. I have an absolute statement here from the department. I will go further. As regards this expenditure in St. John as well as the expenditure in the county of Gloucester during these by-elections, I challenge the Minister of Labour to bring down the pay sheets, to bring down the detailed accounts showing the dates on which the money was spent. Then this house will know who is telling the truth and who is not.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the house just now, because it is almost eleven o'clock. I have more to say, but if I entered now upon other arguments which I wish to advance, and which I shall advance on some other occasion, there would not be time for me to finish. I see by the clock that it is now five minutes to eleven and therefore I will say no more at the moment.
